1a.html:
Coupling of the A and B sites

Cations in an oxide are too far apart for direct exchange; they couple by superexchange through the \mathrm{O^{2-}} between them. The filled O 2p orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin. Each can hop into the d orbital of the cation on its side, and hopping conserves spin, so the two cations end up with opposite spins. The overlap, and so the coupling, depends on the M-O-M angle (Goodenough-Kanamori-Anderson rules):

  • A-O-B at 180^\circ: one p orbital points at both cations, the overlap is largest, and the coupling is strong and antiferromagnetic. Every A is antiparallel to its B neighbours.
  • A-O-A at 90^\circ: the two cations overlap with different, orthogonal p orbitals, so the coupling is weak and, by the GKA rules, ferromagnetic. This agrees with the A-B coupling, which already makes all A moments parallel.
  • No B-O-B bonds: the B moments are coupled only through A, so all B moments are parallel to each other.

The result is two antiparallel sublattices, A up and B down: a ferrimagnet (an antiferromagnet only if the A and B moments were equal). The strong 180^\circ bond fixes a high ordering temperature.

Saturation magnetisation

Given: \mathrm{ABO_2}, A = \mathrm{Fe^{2+}}, B = \mathrm{Co^{2+}}, cubic cell with 4 formula units, a = 0.6\ \mathrm{nm}; \mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\,m^2}.

Solution. Spin-only moments (orbital moment quenched by the crystal field), high-spin ions:

\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}:\ 3d^6,\ 4\ \text{unpaired} \Rightarrow 4\,\mu_B, \qquad \mathrm{Co^{2+}}:\ 3d^7,\ 3\ \text{unpaired} \Rightarrow 3\,\mu_B
\begin{aligned} n_B &= M_A - M_B = 4 - 3 = 1\,\mu_B\ \text{per formula unit} \\ V &= a^3 = (0.6\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m})^3 = 2.16\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ M_s &= \frac{4\,n_B\,\mu_B}{a^3} = \frac{4(1)(9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\,m^2})}{2.16\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m^3}} = 1.72\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}} \end{aligned}

Answer: A and B are coupled antiparallel (ferrimagnetic), with 1\,\mu_B per formula unit and M_s \approx 1.7\times10^{5} A/m (172 kA/m, \mu_0 M_s \approx 0.22 T).

States that the 90^\circ A-O-A coupling is weak (ferromagnetic by the GKA rules) and there is no direct B-B coupling
Concludes that A moments are parallel, B moments are parallel, and A is antiparallel to B: a ferrimagnet
Spin-only moments \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} (3d^6) 4\,\mu_B and \mathrm{Co^{2+}} (3d^7) 3\,\mu_B
Net moment 4 - 3 = 1\,\mu_B per formula unit
Cell volume a^3 = 2.16\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m^3} holding 4 formula units
Uses M_s = (\text{formula units per cell})\,n_B\,\mu_B/a^3
M_s \approx 1.72\times10^{5} A/m with units
Notes the high ordering temperature from the strong 180^\circ bond, or the orbital-moment caveat for \mathrm{Co^{2+}}

1a.watch:
• Do not add the moments (7\,\mu_B): the strongest bond is antiferromagnetic, so the sublattices subtract.
  • Use the high-spin moments; oxide ions give a weak crystal field, so \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} and \mathrm{Co^{2+}} are high spin.
  • \mathrm{Co^{2+}} keeps part of its orbital moment in real oxides (measured \mathrm{CoFe_2O_4} gives about 3.7\,\mu_B rather than 3, 435-mag3 slide 40), so the measured value may differ slightly; the question expects spin-only values.
  • The deck states that 90^\circ bonds give weaker (antiferromagnetic) coupling in spinels, while the GKA slide calls 90^\circ superexchange ferromagnetic. Either way it is weak, and here it does not change the answer, because the 180^\circ A-B bonds dominate.

1b.html:
Given: the \mathrm{ABO_2} oxide of part (a): A = \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} (4\,\mu_B), 4 formula units in a cubic cell with a = 0.6\ \mathrm{nm}, so a^3 = 2.16\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m^3}; \mu_B = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\,m^2}. Each \mu_B per formula unit gives

\frac{4\mu_B}{a^3} = \frac{4(9.27\times10^{-24})}{2.16\times10^{-28}} = 1.717\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}

Find: M_s with B = \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} and with B = \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}.

B = Cu2+

\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} is 3d^9 with one unpaired spin, 1\,\mu_B. The 180^\circ A-O-B superexchange still makes the sublattices antiparallel:

\begin{aligned} n_B &= 4 - 1 = 3\,\mu_B\ \text{per formula unit} \\ M_s &= 3(1.717\times10^{5}) = 5.15\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}} \end{aligned}

B = Zn2+

\mathrm{Zn^{2+}} is 3d^{10}, all spins paired, 0\,\mu_B. The B sublattice carries no moment, so the A-O-B superexchange no longer orders anything. Only the weak 90^\circ A-O-A coupling is left, which is ferromagnetic by the GKA rules, so the \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} moments stay parallel:

\begin{aligned} n_B &= 4\,\mu_B\ \text{per formula unit} \\ M_s &= 4(1.717\times10^{5}) = 6.87\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}} \end{aligned}

Because the 90^\circ coupling is weak, this ferromagnet has a much lower Curie temperature, and the room-temperature magnetisation can be far below the 0 K value.

Answer: Cu on B: 3\,\mu_B per formula unit, M_s \approx 5.2\times10^{5} A/m. Zn on B: 4\,\mu_B per formula unit, M_s \approx 6.9\times10^{5} A/m at low temperature, with a low ordering temperature. Replacing the B moment by a smaller one raises M_s, since B opposes A.
pts: \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} is 3d^9 with 1\,\mu_B
Sublattices still antiparallel, so n_B = 4 - 1 = 3\,\mu_B per formula unit
M_s = 4(3)\mu_B/a^3 \approx 5.15\times10^{5} A/m
\mathrm{Zn^{2+}} is 3d^{10} with no moment, so the A-O-B superexchange no longer couples moments
Only the weak 90^\circ A-O-A coupling remains, ferromagnetic by GKA, so the A moments stay parallel: n_B = 4\,\mu_B
M_s = 4(4)\mu_B/a^3 \approx 6.87\times10^{5} A/m
Notes the low Curie temperature of the Zn compound because the remaining coupling is weak

1b.watch:
• The Zn case is the trap: the A-B antiferromagnetic coupling disappears with the B moment, so the answer depends on the sign of the 90^\circ A-O-A coupling. The GKA slide makes it ferromagnetic (4\,\mu_B); if it were antiferromagnetic, as the deck states for 90^\circ B-O-B bonds in spinels, the A sublattice would order antiferromagnetically and M_s \approx 0. State the rule you use.
  • Do not write 4 - 0 as a ferrimagnet: with no B moment there is no second sublattice to oppose A.
  • Orbital moments of \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} and \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} are taken as quenched (spin-only values).

2a.html:
Storage layer of a hard disk. Data sit in a thin (about 10 to 15 nm) granular film of a hard cobalt alloy, CoCrPt with an oxide (such as \mathrm{SiO_2} or \mathrm{TiO_2}) at the grain boundaries.

  • The grains are hcp Co alloy, about 7 to 9 nm across, with the c-axis (easy axis) normal to the film: perpendicular recording.
  • Pt raises the uniaxial anisotropy K_u (a few 10^5\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}), so the small grains are thermally stable (K_uV \gtrsim 60k_BT).
  • Cr and the oxide segregate to the grain boundaries and break the exchange coupling between grains, so each grain switches as an independent single-domain particle. This keeps the transitions sharp and the noise low.
  • The stack, top down: lubricant, carbon overcoat (2 to 3 nm), CoCrPt-oxide recording layer, Ru interlayer (sets the (0001) texture and grain size), soft magnetic underlayer (returns the head flux), glass or NiP-coated Al-Mg substrate.
  • HAMR disks use \mathrm{L1_0} FePt grains instead (K_u \approx 6.6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}).

2b.html:
The trilemma is three requirements on the recording medium that pull against each other:

  1. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Transitions follow grain boundaries, so each bit needs many grains: SNR rises as \sqrt{N} for N grains per bit. Higher density at the same SNR needs smaller grains (smaller V).
  2. Thermal stability. Each grain must keep its magnetisation for about 10 years, which needs K_uV \gtrsim 60k_BT. Smaller V therefore needs higher K_u.
  3. Writability. The head must switch the grains. The switching field scales with the anisotropy field H_K = 2K_u/\mu_0M_s, but the head field is capped by the saturation of the pole material (FeCo, about 2.4 T). So K_u cannot rise freely.

Small grains plus high K_u means an unwritable medium. For example, CoCrPt (K_u \approx 5\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}) is stable only down to grains of about 8 nm, while \mathrm{L1_0} FePt (K_u \approx 6.6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}) is stable down to about 3.4 nm but has \mu_0H_K \approx 12 T, far beyond any head.

How HAMR solves it. Heat-assisted magnetic recording writes hot and stores cold:

  • The medium is high-K_u \mathrm{L1_0} FePt, with grains small enough for good SNR and stable at room temperature.
  • A laser diode on the slider feeds a plasmonic near-field transducer, which heats a spot tens of nanometres wide to near the Curie temperature of FePt (about 750 K) for about a nanosecond.
  • Near T_C, K_u and H_K collapse, so the ordinary head field writes the hot spot.
  • The spot cools within about a nanosecond while the field is still on, freezing the magnetisation in with the full room-temperature K_u.
  • The steep temperature gradient also sharpens the transitions, which improves SNR.

All three requirements are met together, which is what allows 30 to 50 TB drives.
pts: Names the three competing requirements: SNR, thermal stability and writability

Thermal stability needs K_uV \gtrsim 60k_BT for about 10 years, so smaller grains need higher K_u
Writability: the switching field, about H_K = 2K_u/\mu_0M_s, must stay below the head field, which pole saturation (about 2.4 T) limits
States the conflict with an example: small V and high K_u make the medium unwritable (FePt, \mu_0H_K \approx 12 T)
HAMR uses a high-K_u \mathrm{L1_0} FePt medium whose grains are stable at a few nanometres
A laser and near-field transducer heat a small spot near T_C (about 750 K) for about a nanosecond, so K_u and H_K fall and the head field can write
Rapid cooling in the field freezes the bit at the full room-temperature K_u; the thermal gradient sharpens transitions
Concludes that all three requirements are met together, enabling 30 to 50 TB drives

2b.watch:
• The grain sizes quoted are cube edges from V = 60k_BT/K_u at 300 K: 5.0\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{m^3} for CoCrPt and 3.8\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{m^3} for FePt. Real CoCrPt grains are columns about 8 nm wide and 12 nm tall, about 73k_BT.
  • The slides' 25k_BT rule is for laboratory times; storage for years under the fields of neighbouring bits needs about 60k_BT (O'Handley).
  • The heating must not spread: the lubricant and carbon overcoat degrade when hot, and heat reaching the next track would erase it. This is why the hot spot is so small and so short.
  • Another answer to the trilemma is microwave-assisted recording (MAMR), which lowers the switching field with a microwave field instead of heat.

2c.html:
Magnetocrystalline anisotropy needs two ingredients at the magnetic ion: an orbital moment (L \neq 0, a non-spherical electron cloud) and a crystal field that favours some orientations of that cloud. Spin-orbit coupling (\xi\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{S}) then ties the spin, and so \mathbf{M}, to the lattice.

The 4f shell is shielded by the filled 5s and 5p shells, so spin-orbit coupling beats the crystal field and L is not quenched. Rotating \mathbf{M} drags the 4f cloud against the crystal field, which costs energy.

  • \mathrm{Gd^{3+}}, 4f^7: the shell is half filled, S = 7/2 and L = 0. The cloud is spherical, so the crystal field cannot sense the spin direction: K_u is very small.
  • \mathrm{Tb^{3+}} (4f^8, L = 3) and \mathrm{Dy^{3+}} (4f^9, L = 5): large orbital moments and strongly aspherical clouds give high K_u, and also large magnetostriction.
pts: Anisotropy needs an orbital moment (non-spherical cloud, L \neq 0) plus a crystal field, linked to the spin by spin-orbit coupling
In 4f ions spin-orbit coupling exceeds the crystal field (shielded 4f shell), so L is not quenched
\mathrm{Gd^{3+}} is 4f^7, half filled, L = 0 (S-state), spherical: very low K_u
\mathrm{Tb^{3+}} (L = 3) and \mathrm{Dy^{3+}} (L = 5) have large orbital moments, so high K_u
2c.watch:
• Gd still has a large moment (7\,\mu_B, all spin); the point is the absence of orbital moment, not of magnetism.
  • The same reason makes Tb and Dy compounds (for example Terfenol-D, \mathrm{Tb_{0.3}Dy_{0.7}Fe_2}) giant magnetostrictors, while Gd compounds have small magnetostriction.

3a.html:
Given: \mathrm{Nd_3Ga_5O_{12}} (NGG) substrate, (111), a_s = 12.505 Å; the printed lattice parameters and \lambda_{100}, \lambda_{111} of the rare-earth iron garnets \mathrm{RE_3Fe_5O_{12}}. Not printed, so assumed: garnet E \approx 200 GPa, \nu \approx 0.29.

Find: the garnet film most likely to be magnetised out of plane.

Solution

Step 1, strain from the misfit. A thin coherent film takes the substrate's in-plane spacing, so it carries a biaxial strain and stress

\varepsilon = \frac{a_s - a_f}{a_f}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{E}{1 - \nu}\,\varepsilon \approx 2.8\times10^{11}\,\varepsilon\ \mathrm{Pa}

NGG has a larger cell than every film except Sm, so almost every film is in tension (\varepsilon > 0).

Step 2, magnetoelastic anisotropy of a (111) film. The normal [111] is a threefold axis, so an in-plane biaxial stress gives a uniaxial anisotropy about the normal, set by \lambda_{111}. With E = K_{me}\sin^2\theta, \theta measured from the normal (K_{me} > 0 means the normal is easy):

K_{me} = -\tfrac{3}{2}\lambda_{111}\,\sigma

A film in tension needs \lambda_{111} < 0; a compressed film needs \lambda_{111} > 0.

Step 3, screen the table (\lambda_{111} in 10^{-6}):

Sm12.530−0.20−8.5-7.2\times10^{3}no
Eu12.498+0.06+1.8-4\times10^{2}no
Gd12.470+0.28−2.9+3.4\times10^{3}weak
Tb12.436+0.55+12-2.8\times10^{4}no, strongly in plane
Dy12.405+0.81−5.9+2.0\times10^{4}yes
Ho12.375+1.05−3.4+1.5\times10^{4}yes
Er12.349+1.26−4.9+2.6\times10^{4}yes, misfit above 1 %
Tm12.325+1.46−5.2+3.2\times10^{4}yes, misfit above 1 %
Yb12.302+1.65−4.5+3.1\times10^{4}yes, misfit above 1 %

Step 4, choose. DyIG has the most negative \lambda_{111} of the films in tension (-5.9\times10^{-6}; SmIG's -8.5 is wasted because SmIG is compressed) under a moderate tension of 0.81 % (\sigma \approx 2.3 GPa), giving K_{me} \approx 2.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}. That exceeds even the shape anisotropy of YIG (\mu_0 M_s^2/2 \approx 1.2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}} for M_s \approx 140\ \mathrm{kA\,m^{-1}}), and DyIG's own moment at 300 K is far smaller because its compensation point lies near 220 K. Er, Tm and Yb reach a larger K_{me} only through misfits of 1.3 to 1.7 %. The critical thickness falls roughly as 1/misfit, so these tensile films relax (misfit dislocations or cracks) at half to two-thirds of DyIG's thickness and lose the strain.

Answer: grow a thin (tens of nm), coherently strained \mathrm{Dy_3Fe_5O_{12}} film on NGG (111): 0.81 % in-plane tension, \lambda_{111} = -5.9\times10^{-6}, K_{me} \approx +2.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}, so the easy axis is the film normal. TmIG would give the largest K_{me} (3.2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}) if it stayed coherent at 1.46 %; a (Dy,Tm) garnet can trade misfit against anisotropy.

• This paper prints no equation sheet: remember K_{me} = -\frac{3}{2}\lambda_{111}\sigma for a (111) film, \lambda_{100} for a (100) film and \lambda_{110} = \frac{1}{4}\lambda_{100} + \frac{3}{4}\lambda_{111} for a (110) film.

3b.html:
Principle. An arriving atom joins the crystal without a defect only if it diffuses to a ledge or kink (slides 32-33, 68) before later atoms bury it. Otherwise it is frozen in as a vacancy, void, misoriented cluster (grain boundary) or amorphous material; gas molecules that stick become impurity defects. The three process parameters (slide 34) act through

\delta_{ad} = \left(\frac{N_0 D_0}{F_{\mathrm{dep}}}\right)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta g^*_{SD}}{2kT_{\mathrm{sub}}}\right), \qquad x_i = \frac{F_i}{F_{\mathrm{dep}} + F_i}

Source temperature. p_{\mathrm{eq}} = K_0^{\prime}\exp(-h_{\mathrm{evap}}/RT_{\mathrm{sor}}) and F_{\mathrm{dep}} \propto \bar{R}_e \propto p_{\mathrm{eq}}, so the flux rises exponentially: for example, with h_{\mathrm{evap}} = 150\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}, going from 1200 to 1300 K triples it. A higher flux shortens the time between arrivals, \tau_{ad} = N_0/F_{\mathrm{dep}}, so \delta_{ad} \propto F_{\mathrm{dep}}^{-1/2} falls (here by 44%) and nucleation rises: more vacancies, voids and grain boundaries, and growth moves from epitaxial to polycrystalline to amorphous (slides 20, 75). But x_i \approx F_i/F_{\mathrm{dep}} falls, so the film is purer (slide 38).

Substrate temperature. D_{SD} = D_0\exp(-\Delta g^*_{SD}/kT_{\mathrm{sub}}) rises, so \delta_{ad} rises: atoms reach ledges and kinks, grains grow, and once T_{\mathrm{sub}} crosses the epitaxy line for the rate used (slide 20) the film grows single-crystal. Weakly bound gas also desorbs. Too hot, growth becomes desorption-limited: \delta_{de} \propto \exp[(\Delta g^*_d - \Delta g^*_{SD})/2kT_{\mathrm{sub}}] falls and atoms re-evaporate. Defect density is lowest near the temperature where \delta peaks.

Background pressure. F_i = 3.513\times10^{22}\,p_{\mathrm{back}}/\sqrt{MT} rises linearly with p_{\mathrm{back}}, raising x_i: oxygen and water give impurity defects and oxides at boundaries, and adsorbed gas blocks surface diffusion. If every molecule sticks at 1 monolayer per second of growth, x_i \approx 4\% at 10^{-7} Torr but 0.04\% at 10^{-9} Torr (slide 45). When \lambda \approx 5\times10^{-3}/p_{\mathrm{back}} cm falls below H, gas scattering gives oblique arrival and porous, shadowed columns.

Conclusion. Few defects need ultra-high vacuum (bake-out, load-lock), a moderate T_{\mathrm{sor}} that still keeps F_{\mathrm{dep}} \gg F_i, and a high T_{\mathrm{sub}} near the peak of \delta, short of the desorption-limited range.
pts: Principle: an adatom must reach a ledge or kink within its diffusion distance before burial, otherwise vacancies, voids, grain boundaries or amorphous film; stuck gas gives impurity defects
Names the controlling quantities: \delta_{ad} = (N_0 D_{SD}/F_{\mathrm{dep}})^{1/2} and x_i = F_i/(F_{\mathrm{dep}} + F_i)
T_{\mathrm{sor}} up: p_{\mathrm{eq}} and F_{\mathrm{dep}} rise exponentially, \delta_{ad} \propto F_{\mathrm{dep}}^{-1/2} falls, so more structural defects, finer grains, poly or amorphous growth
T_{\mathrm{sor}} up also lowers the impurity fraction (F_{\mathrm{evap}} \gg F_{\mathrm{impurity}}), giving a purer film
T_{\mathrm{sub}} up: D_{SD} and \delta_{ad} rise, so atoms reach ledges and kinks; fewer defects, larger grains, epitaxy possible
T_{\mathrm{sub}} too high: desorption-limited \delta_{de} falls (since \Delta g^*_d > \Delta g^*_{SD}) and atoms re-evaporate, so there is an optimum
p_{\mathrm{back}} up: F_i \propto p_{\mathrm{back}} raises x_i; impurity defects, and adsorbed gas hinders surface diffusion
A number: x_i about 4% at 10^{-7} Torr against 0.04% at 10^{-9} Torr at 1 monolayer per second, or similar
High p_{\mathrm{back}}: \lambda < H, gas scattering, oblique arrival and porous columns
Conclusion: UHV, moderate T_{\mathrm{sor}}, high T_{\mathrm{sub}} below the desorption regime

4a.html:
Given: a small amount of \mathrm{CuCl_2} dissolved in rock-salt NaCl (one Na site per Cl site); Na diffuses by jumping into Na vacancies.

Find: the defect reaction, and D_{\mathrm{Na}} in the intrinsic and extrinsic regimes.

Step 1, solution reaction. \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} on a \mathrm{Na^+} site has an effective charge of +1, \mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}. Its two Cl ions fill two Cl sites, so two Na sites are used and the second stays empty:

\mathrm{CuCl_2} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{NaCl}\ } \mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}} + 2\mathrm{Cl_{Cl}^{ imes}}

Mass: one Cu and two Cl on each side. Sites: 2 Na to 2 Cl. Charge: (+1) + (-1) = 0.

Step 2, intrinsic (Schottky) equilibrium.

ext{null} ightleftharpoons \mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}} + \mathrm{V_{Cl}^{ ullet}}, \qquad K_s = [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}][\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{ ullet}}] = \exp\left( rac{\Delta S_s}{k} ight)\exp\left(- rac{\Delta H_s}{kT} ight)

Step 3, electroneutrality.

[\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}] + [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{ ullet}}] \quad\Rightarrow\quad [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = rac{[\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}]}{2} + \sqrt{ rac{[\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}]^2}{4} + K_s}

Step 4, diffusion coefficient. Each Na jump needs a vacancy beside it, so D_{\mathrm{Na}} is proportional to the vacancy fraction:

D_{\mathrm{Na}} = \gamma a^2 u\,[\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}]\exp\left( rac{\Delta S_m}{k} ight)\exp\left(- rac{\Delta H_m}{kT} ight)

Intrinsic regime (high T, [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{ ullet}}] \gg [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}]): [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = K_s^{1/2}, so

oxed{D_{\mathrm{Na}} = D_0\exp\left(- rac{\Delta H_m + \Delta H_s/2}{kT} ight)}, \qquad D_0 = \gamma a^2 u\exp\left( rac{\Delta S_m + \Delta S_s/2}{k} ight)

Extrinsic regime (low T, [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}] \gg [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{ ullet}}]): [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}], fixed by the solute, so

oxed{D_{\mathrm{Na}} = D_0^{\prime}\,[\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}]\exp\left(- rac{\Delta H_m}{kT} ight)}, \qquad D_0^{\prime} = \gamma a^2 u\exp\left( rac{\Delta S_m}{k} ight)

Answer: the Arrhenius plot is two straight lines, slope -(\Delta H_m + \Delta H_s/2)/k at high T and -\Delta H_m/k at low T. They meet where K_s^{1/2} = [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{ ullet}}], about 535^\circ\mathrm{C} for the data given. More \mathrm{CuCl_2} raises the extrinsic line and moves the knee to a higher temperature.
pts: Reaction \mathrm{CuCl_2} \to \mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}} + 2\mathrm{Cl_{Cl}^{\times}}

Electroneutrality [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{\bullet}}] + [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{\bullet}}]
Vacancy mechanism: D_{\mathrm{Na}} = \gamma a^2\nu[\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}]\exp(-\Delta G_m/kT), proportional to [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}]
Intrinsic: [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = K_s^{1/2}, D = D_0\exp[-(\Delta H_m + \Delta H_s/2)/kT]
Extrinsic: [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{\bullet}}], D = D_0^{\prime}[\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{\bullet}}]\exp(-\Delta H_m/kT)

4b.html:
Given: the fitted line of the Arrhenius plot; k = R/F = 8.615\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}} (printed).

Find: the migration enthalpy \Delta H_m of the Na vacancy.

Solution. In the low-temperature extrinsic regime [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cu_{Na}^{\bullet}}] is constant, so \ln D = \text{const} - \Delta H_m/kT and the slope of \ln D against 1/T is -\Delta H_m/k.

Two points on the extrinsic line, read where it crosses the decade gridlines of the figure: D_1 = 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} at 1/T_1 = 1.36\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} (735 K) and D_2 = 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} at 1/T_2 = 1.62\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} (617 K).

\begin{aligned} \Delta H_m &= \frac{k\ln(D_1/D_2)}{1/T_2 - 1/T_1} \\ &= \frac{(8.615\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}})(\ln 10)}{(1.62 - 1.36)\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}} \\ &= \frac{1.984\times10^{-4}}{2.6\times10^{-4}}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.763\ \mathrm{eV} \end{aligned}

In molar units, 0.763 \times 96.5 = 73.6\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.

Answer: \Delta H_m \approx 0.76\ \mathrm{eV} per jump (about 74\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}), read from the figure.

Uses the printed k = 8.615\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}} and the 10^{-3} of the axis
Final \Delta H_m \approx 0.76\ \mathrm{eV} (accept 0.73 to 0.79 eV)

4c.html:
Given: the fitted line of the Arrhenius plot; k = 8.615\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}}; \Delta H_m = 0.763\ \mathrm{eV} from part (b).

Find: the Schottky formation enthalpy \Delta H_s.

Solution. In the high-temperature intrinsic regime [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = K_s^{1/2}, so the activation energy is Q_{\mathrm{int}} = \Delta H_m + \Delta H_s/2.

Two points on the intrinsic line, read where it crosses the gridlines: 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} at 1/T = 1.07\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} (935 K) and 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} at 1.18\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} (847 K).

\begin{aligned} Q_{\mathrm{int}} &= \frac{(8.615\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}})(\ln 10)}{(1.18 - 1.07)\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}} = 1.80\ \mathrm{eV} \\ \Delta H_s &= 2\left(Q_{\mathrm{int}} - \Delta H_m\right) = 2(1.803 - 0.763)\ \mathrm{eV} = 2.08\ \mathrm{eV} \end{aligned}

Answer: \Delta H_s \approx 2.1\ \mathrm{eV} per Schottky pair (201\ \mathrm{kJ} per mole of pairs), about 1.04 eV per vacancy, read from the figure. This is close to the 1.15 eV per defect (2.3 eV per pair) that slide 9 lists for NaCl.
pts: States that in the intrinsic regime Q = \Delta H_m + \Delta H_s/2, because [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = K_s^{1/2}
Reads two points on the steep line, about (1.06\text{ to }1.07\times10^{-3}, 10^{-9}) and (1.17\text{ to }1.18\times10^{-3}, 10^{-10}), one decade apart over 0.11\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}
Intrinsic activation energy Q_{\mathrm{int}} \approx 1.80\ \mathrm{eV}
\Delta H_s = 2(Q_{\mathrm{int}} - \Delta H_m) \approx 2.1\ \mathrm{eV} (accept 2.0 to 2.2 eV)
States that the value is per Schottky pair (about 1.04 eV per vacancy)
Compares with the tabulated 2.3 eV per pair for NaCl and calls the agreement reasonable

5a.html:
Film quality (density, defects, adhesion, stress, coverage, uniformity, stoichiometry, purity, crystallinity; slide 4) differs because of three things:

  • Energy of arriving atoms: evaporated atoms carry about kT_{\mathrm{sor}}, 0.1 to 0.2 eV; sputtered atoms 3 to 10 eV, plus reflected Ar neutrals and ions.
  • Pressure: evaporation runs at 10^{-5} to 10^{-10} Torr (\lambda \gg H); sputtering in 1 to 100 mTorr of Ar, with gas collisions.
  • Source: a small hot source against an extended, cool target.
QualityEvaporated filmSputtered film
Density, microstructurelow-energy atoms barely diffuse: porous Zone 1 columns unless the substrate is heatedbombardment densifies the film and raises surface diffusivity (slide 31); dense Zone T
Adhesionweakergenerally good: energetic atoms clean and mix the interface
Stressusually tensilecompressive at low Ar pressure (peening), tensile at high pressure
Step coverage, uniformityline of sight: shadowed steps; uniformity needs a large Hwide arrival angles: better coverage and uniformity, not as good as CVD
Stoichiometryalloys fractionate, compounds dissociate; needs several sourcesfilm = target composition at steady state
Purityhighest: UHV, no working gasAr and gas impurities incorporated; needs pure, gettered gas
Defectsfew bombardment defectssubsurface damage from energetic particles
Crystallinityepitaxy possible (MBE: slow, UHV, atomic control)good for polycrystalline and amorphous films, not for epitaxy

Conclusion. Sputtered films are denser, adhere better, cover steps more evenly and keep the composition of alloy and compound targets. Evaporated films are purer and can be epitaxial, but are porous and shadowed unless the substrate is heated and rotated.

Adhesion better for sputtered films (interface cleaned and mixed)
Stress: sputtered compressive at low Ar pressure (peening), tensile at high; evaporated usually tensile
Step coverage and thickness uniformity better for sputtering (extended source, wide arrival angles); evaporation is line of sight with shadowing
Stoichiometry: sputtered film keeps the target composition; evaporation fractionates alloys and dissociates compounds
Purity: evaporated films purer (UHV, no working gas); sputtered films incorporate Ar and impurities

• "Differentiate" needs both sides for each property; a table is the fastest way to show it.
  • The slides list "higher energies" as both a plus (higher surface diffusivity) and a minus (subsurface defects); give both.
  • Stress depends on the Ar pressure: at low pressure reflected Ar neutrals peen the film and are trapped in it (compressive); at high pressure scattering removes that energy, so films are tensile and more porous.

5b.html:
DC limitation. The DC target is the cathode and must conduct: on an insulator the \mathrm{Ar^+} charge cannot drain away, the surface potential rises, the field collapses and sputtering stops, often with arcing.

Benefits of RF (13.56 MHz, through a matching network and blocking capacitor; slide 80):

  1. Insulators and any other material can be sputtered. The RF voltage couples through the target's capacitance. Electrons are far more mobile than ions, so during the short positive part of each cycle they neutralise the charge, and the target self-biases negative for almost the whole cycle; ions keep sputtering it.
  2. Dielectric and oxide films straight from compound targets: \mathrm{SiO_2}, \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, ZnO, AlN, PZT for capacitors, piezoelectric and optical layers.
  3. Better ionisation at lower pressure. Electrons oscillating in the field gain enough energy to ionise, so the discharge does not depend on secondary electrons and runs at about 0.5 to 10 mTorr: less scattering, less trapped Ar, denser films.
  4. Fewer charging problems: no charge build-up or arcing on oxidised (poisoned) targets or insulating substrates; RF bias also allows sputter-cleaning of substrates.

The price: a more complex, costly supply and lower rates than DC for metals.
pts: DC limitation: insulating target charges positive under ion bombardment, the field collapses and sputtering stops; DC needs a conducting target
RF sputters insulators (and any material): capacitive coupling, electrons neutralise the charge in the brief positive part, the target self-biases negative
Dielectric and oxide films deposited directly, with examples (\mathrm{SiO_2}, \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, ZnO, PZT)
Higher ionisation efficiency (electrons gain energy in the RF field); operation at lower pressure, less scattering and gas incorporation, denser films
No arcing on poisoned targets or insulating substrates; RF bias for substrate cleaning
Names 13.56 MHz and the matching network, and notes the trade-off (cost, lower rate)
5b.src: Ceramic processing: thin-film deposition, slides 78, 80; Sputter deposition, slides 3-4; Ohring, The Materials Science of Thin Films, 2nd ed., pp 235-239
5b.watch:
• The self-bias is the key idea: without it an AC target would sputter only half the time and the substrate as much as the target. It needs a blocking capacitor (or an insulating target) so no DC current can flow.
  • 13.56 MHz is chosen because it is a frequency allotted to industrial plasma use, and it is high enough (above about 1 MHz) that ions cannot follow the field while electrons can.
  • RF-sputtered oxides tend to be oxygen-deficient; a little \mathrm{O_2} is added, or reactive DC sputtering from a metal target is used instead.

5c.html:
Sputtering gives dense, adherent, well-covered films, but it has these concerns (slide 82 and beyond):

  1. Damage from energetic particles. Sputtered atoms (3 to 10 eV), reflected Ar neutrals and negative ions create subsurface defects, mix the interface and resputter the film, so it is not used for epitaxy.
  2. Gas incorporation and purity. It runs in 1 to 100 mTorr of Ar, so Ar and impurity gases (\mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{H_2O}) are built into the film; very pure or gettered gas and a low base pressure are needed.
  3. Stress. At low pressure, peening by Ar neutrals and trapped Ar give compressive stress (buckling, delamination); at high pressure films are porous and tensile.
  4. Low rate and efficiency. About 10^{16} against 10^{17} atoms \mathrm{cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}} for evaporation; most power heats the target; gas scattering cuts the rate at high pressure, hence magnetrons.
  5. Substrate heating by condensation energy, energetic atoms and plasma electrons (about 160 °C in a minute for 1 μm of Al), harmful to polymers and resists.
  6. Target problems. Magnetron racetrack erosion wastes most of the target and spoils uniformity; brittle ceramic targets crack; reactive sputtering poisons the target (hysteresis).
  7. Insulators need RF: costly, slower, often metal-rich. Non-directional arrival also makes lift-off patterning difficult.
pts: Energetic-particle damage: subsurface defects, interface mixing and resputtering; unsuitable for epitaxy
Gas incorporation: Ar and impurity gases trapped at 1 to 100 mTorr; needs pure, gettered gas and good base vacuum
Stress: compressive from peening and trapped Ar at low pressure, porous and tensile at high pressure; risk of cracking or delamination
Low deposition rate and power efficiency compared with evaporation; rate falls with gas scattering; magnetron needed
Substrate heating by bombardment and plasma
Target concerns: racetrack erosion (poor utilisation, uniformity), cracking of ceramic targets, poisoning in reactive sputtering
Insulators need costly, slower RF; non-directional flux is poor for lift-off

5c.watch:
• The slides' own list (slide 82) is short: subsurface defects, gas incorporation, not good for epitaxy. Lead with those, then add the process concerns.
  • Several items are trade-offs: the energy that causes damage also densifies the film, and the wide arrival angles that spoil lift-off give better step coverage.
  • The 160 °C figure is Ohring's estimate for a thermally isolated 0.5 mm Si wafer coated with 1 μm of Al in 60 s.

6a.html:
Most working layers of a microsystem are polycrystalline: they are deposited at low temperature on amorphous or patterned layers (oxide, nitride, other metals), where there is no single-crystal template, so islands nucleate in many orientations and meet at grain boundaries (Volmer-Weber, slide 8). Their grain size, texture and grain boundaries (\gamma_{gb} \approx 0.1\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}) then decide how the device works (slide 10).

Application (slide 4)Polycrystalline filmsWhat the grain structure does
IC conductors: interconnects, vias, contactsAl or Cu lines, W plugs, TiN or TaN barriers and glue layers, silicides, set in amorphous \mathrm{SiO_2} and SiNboundaries are fast diffusion paths (electromigration voids, barrier leakage) and scatter electrons (higher resistivity in narrow lines); large "bamboo" grains and (111) texture are wanted
MOSFET gatesdoped polysilicon, often silicidedconducts and survives high-temperature steps (self-aligned gate); boundary trapping raises resistance
Thin-film transistors (displays, memories)poly-Si channel on glasscarrier scattering, trapped charge and mid-gap states: mobility about 10 to 100 \mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}, between a-Si (about 1) and crystalline Si (1350)
Magnetic media, read/write heads, MRAMgranular Co-alloy media, NiFe and CoFe layersboundaries pin domain walls and isolate grains: high coercivity and small bits in media; in soft head layers pinning is unwanted
MEMS: accelerometers, gyroscopes, pressure gauges, microengines, sensorsLPCVD poly-Si beams on sacrificial \mathrm{SiO_2}, metal filmsboundaries strengthen the film; residual stress and stress gradients curl released beams, so deposition and annealing are tuned
Photonics: micromirror optical switchesAl-coated mirrors on poly-Sifine grains keep the mirror smooth and limit light scattering

Control. Grain size rises with substrate temperature and falls with deposition rate, \bar{d} = f(\delta, \dot{N}, G); annealing grows grains until they stagnate at \bar{d} \approx h; abnormal growth gives (111) texture in thin fcc films (surface energy) and (100) in thick, strained ones.
pts: Why polycrystalline: low-temperature deposition on amorphous or patterned layers with no single-crystal template; properties set by grain size, texture and boundaries
Grain-boundary effects: carrier scattering (lower mobility), mid-gap states, trapped charge (barrier to conduction), fast diffusion; also strengthening, light scattering, domain pinning
Interconnects, vias, barriers, silicides named (Al, Cu, W, TiN, silicides), with electromigration or resistivity explained and large-grain or (111) structure wanted
Polysilicon gates and TFTs: boundary trapping and scattering, mobility between amorphous and crystalline Si
Magnetic media, heads and MRAM: boundaries pin and isolate domains, setting coercivity and bit size
MEMS: poly-Si structural layers, strengthened by boundaries; residual stress and its gradient must be controlled
Photonics: smooth, fine-grained micromirrors for optical switching
Control of grain size and texture by substrate temperature, deposition rate, annealing and abnormal grain growth

6b.fix: • Slide 9 of the second epitaxy deck says the strain energy "per volume" of a coherent film increases with thickness. The energy per unit volume, Y\varepsilon^2, is constant in a uniformly strained film; what increases is the energy per unit area, E_\varepsilon = \varepsilon^2 Y h, as slide 13 of the same deck writes it.
6b.html:
Pseudomorphic growth means the film adopts the crystal structure and in-plane lattice parameter of the substrate, so the interface is coherent. The misfit is taken up entirely as elastic strain, the pseudomorphic strain:

f = rac{a_s - a_f}{a_f} = \varepsilon \qquad (\delta = 0)

The cell is squeezed or stretched in-plane and changes the opposite way normal to the interface: a cubic film becomes tetragonal (slide 8). f > 0 puts the film in tension; SiGe on Si (a_f > a_s) is in compression. The biaxial coherency stress and the strain energy per unit area are

\sigma = Y\varepsilon = Y\, rac{a_s - a_f}{a_f}, \qquad Y = rac{E}{1- u}, \qquad E_\varepsilon = \varepsilon^2 Y h

Thickness limit. E_\varepsilon grows linearly with thickness h, because the whole film volume is strained. Misfit dislocations cost energy only at the interface, E_d, which grows only weakly with h. At the critical thickness h_c the two cross, and thicker films are cheaper with dislocations: the film becomes semi-coherent and part of the misfit is plastic, f = \varepsilon + \delta with \delta = b_{\mathrm{eff}}/S. Minimising E_\varepsilon + E_d gives the largest elastic strain a film of thickness h can hold,

\varepsilon^* = rac{ ilde{G}(1- u\cos^2\alpha)(b/b_{\mathrm{eff}})[\ln(h/b)+1]}{2Yh}

which falls as h rises. Growth is pseudomorphic while f < \varepsilon^*; setting f = \varepsilon^* gives

h_c = rac{ ilde{G}(1- u\cos^2\alpha)(b/b_{\mathrm{eff}})[\ln(h_c/b)+1]}{2Yf}

so h_c varies roughly as 1/f: about 100 Å at 1% misfit. Above h_c the elastic strain and stress fall along \varepsilon^* and \delta rises towards f.
pts: Pseudomorphic growth: film takes the substrate's in-plane lattice parameter, coherent interface, all misfit elastic, \varepsilon = f = (a_s - a_f)/a_f
Tetragonal distortion: in-plane strain with the opposite normal strain; sign gives tension or compression
Coherency stress \sigma = Y\varepsilon with biaxial modulus Y = E/(1-\nu)
Strain energy per area E_\varepsilon = Y\varepsilon^2 h grows linearly with h; dislocation energy is interfacial and only weakly thickness dependent
Beyond the crossing, misfit dislocations form: f = \varepsilon + \delta, \delta = b_{\mathrm{eff}}/S, the film becomes semi-coherent and its stress decays
h_c from f = \varepsilon^* with \varepsilon^* falling with h; h_c \sim 1/f, about 100 Å at 1% misfit

6c.html:
The critical transition temperature T_c is the temperature below which a material loses all electrical resistance and expels magnetic flux (slides 2, 11). Its significance:

  1. Boundary between two states. Above T_c the material is a normal metal (or even an insulator); below it \rho = 0, so a current persists, and B = 0 inside (Meissner). The transition is reversible. It is sharp for pure metals and 1 to 2 K wide for alloys and ceramics, because of composition and oxygen-content variations, grain boundaries, porosity and strain (slide 11).
  2. Pairing and the energy gap. Below T_c electrons form Cooper pairs and a gap opens, reaching 2\Delta(0) \approx 3.52k_BT_c at 0 K; as T rises pairs break, and at T_c the gap vanishes (slide 10).
  3. It bounds the other critical limits. The critical field, and with it the critical current, falls to zero at T_c:
H_c(T) = H_c(0)\left[1 - \left(\frac{T}{T_c}\right)^2\right]

At T = T_c/2 only 75% of H_c(0) remains, so devices run well below T_c.

  1. It fixes the coolant and cost. Hg (4.15 K), Nb (9.2 K) and \mathrm{Nb_3Sn} (18.3 K) need liquid helium (4.2 K); \mathrm{YBa_2Cu_3O_7} (92 K) and Tl-Ba-Ca-Cu-O (125 K) work in liquid nitrogen (77 K), which is far cheaper (slides 12, 15, 23).
  2. It depends on the lattice. The isotope effect, M^{\alpha}T_c = \text{const}, shows that phonons take part in pairing in metals.

7a.html:
A dielectric ceramic is an insulator: a field cannot drive charge through it, but it shifts bound charges by small distances and so creates dipoles, \mu = q\delta. The polarisation is the dipole moment per unit volume:

P = \frac{\sum\mu}{V} = N\mu = N\alpha E = \varepsilon_0(\varepsilon_r - 1)E \quad (\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}})

where \alpha = \mu/E is the polarisability. Four mechanisms can act, and their effects add: P = P_e + P_i + P_d + P_s.

1. Electronic polarisation. In every atom or ion the field pulls the electron cloud one way and the nucleus the other, so their centres separate by \delta. The applied force ZeE is balanced by the Coulomb pull of the displaced cloud, Z^2e^2\delta/(4\pi\varepsilon_0R^3), which gives

\alpha_e = 4\pi\varepsilon_0R^3

Large ions are therefore the most polarisable (\mathrm{O^{2-}}, \mathrm{I^-} > \mathrm{F^-}). It occurs in all materials and is the only mechanism in covalent diamond and Si, where \varepsilon_r = n^2. Electrons are light, so it follows the field up to about 10^{15} Hz (ultraviolet).

2. Ionic polarisation. In ionic ceramics (MgO, \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, NaCl) cations move with the field and anions against it. The bonds act as springs of stiffness k_i = Yd_0, so qE = k_id and

\alpha_i = \frac{q^2}{Yd_0}

Stiff, high-melting bonds polarise less. NaCl has \varepsilon_r = 5.9 against n^2 = 2.37, so the ionic term adds about 3.5. Ions are heavier, so it lasts only to about 10^{13} Hz (infrared).

3. Dipolar (orientation) polarisation. Some units carry permanent dipoles: adsorbed \mathrm{H_2O} or OH groups in porous ceramics and glasses, dopant-vacancy pairs that reorient by ion jumps, and the off-centre \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} of \mathrm{BaTiO_3}. With no field they point at random (\sum\mu = 0); the field turns them, against thermal agitation:

\alpha_d = \frac{\mu^2}{3kT}

so this term falls as temperature rises. It is large (water 80; coupled dipoles give \mathrm{BaTiO_3} \kappa in the thousands), but rotation is slow: it relaxes at about 10^{7} to 10^{9} Hz.

4. Space-charge (interfacial) polarisation. Mobile ions or electrons from impurities and defects drift through a grain until they are stopped at a grain boundary, pore, second phase or electrode. Positive and negative charges pile up on opposite sides, so each grain becomes one large dipole. The displacement is the largest of the four, so \varepsilon_r can be very high, but the motion is slow (below about 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz) and lossy, and it grows with impurity content and temperature.

Overall. The slowest mechanism drops out first as frequency rises, so \varepsilon_r falls in steps: f_{\mathrm{interfacial}} < f_{\mathrm{dipolar}} < f_{\mathrm{ionic}} < f_{\mathrm{electronic}}.

7b.fix: Slide 18 lists a "paper-based piezoresistive force sensor" under piezoelectric power sources (mechanical to electrical). A piezoresistive sensor only changes its resistance under strain and needs an external supply; it generates no charge. 7b.html:
A poled piezoelectric ceramic (PZT, \mathrm{BaTiO_3}) converts energy both ways (slide 16):

\text{direct: } D = dT + \varepsilon E, \qquad \text{indirect (converse): } S = dE

High-d ceramics suit actuators and high-g (g = d/\varepsilon) ones suit voltage generators. Slide 16: d \approx 250 to 365 pC/N for PZT, 100 to 149 for \mathrm{BaTiO_3}, 2.3 for quartz.

Direct effect: mechanical to electrical (generators, sensors)

  • Spark igniters in gas lighters, gas stoves and welding torches: a quick blow on a PZT cylinder gives a high-voltage spark (about 3 mJ).
  • Pressure and force sensors, accelerometers (airbag and seat-belt systems), knock sensors.
  • Microphones, hydrophones, record pickups and strain gauges.
  • Energy harvesting from vibration or footsteps.

Indirect effect: electrical to mechanical (actuators)

  • Nanopositioners: AFM and STM scanners, lens and mirror alignment, precision machine tools (strain about 0.1%, so nanometre steps).
  • Piezo inkjet print heads and fuel injectors.
  • Buzzers, loudspeakers, ultrasonic cleaners and drills (an AC field makes the ceramic vibrate).

Both effects in one device

  • Ultrasonic transducers for medical imaging (2 to 30 MHz), sonar and flaw detection: the element sends a pulse (indirect) and detects the echo (direct).
  • Resonators and frequency filters.

8a.html:
(i) Metal loss from ZnO

Zn leaves as a neutral vapour atom, taking two electrons with it. Leaving a lattice site creates a neutral zinc vacancy, which then ionises into the valence band:

\mathrm{Zn_{Zn}^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zn(g)} + \mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\times}}, \qquad \mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime}} + h^{\bullet}, \qquad \mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime\prime}} + h^{\bullet}
\text{Overall:}\quad \mathrm{Zn_{Zn}^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zn(g)} + \mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}

Mass: one Zn each side. Sites: the Zn site remains (now empty), so Zn : O stays 1 : 1. Charge: -2 + 2 = 0. With K_1 = p_{\mathrm{Zn}}[\mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime\prime}}]p^2 and p = 2[\mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime\prime}}], [\mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime\prime}}] = (K_1/4)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{Zn}}^{-1/3}. The same change written with oxygen is \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_{Zn}^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}, a metal-deficient, p-type \mathrm{Zn_{1-x}O}.

Real ZnO is metal-excess, \mathrm{Zn_{1+x}O} with \mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}} donors, so metal loss first removes these interstitials and their electrons:

\mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}} + e^{\prime} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Zn(g)}, \qquad n = [\mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}}] \propto p_{\mathrm{Zn}}^{1/2}

The n-type conductivity therefore falls as Zn is lost.

(ii) Dissolution of \mathrm{Nb_2O_5} in \mathrm{TiO_2}

\mathrm{Nb^{5+}} on a \mathrm{Ti^{4+}} site is a donor, \mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}}. Two Nb need only four O sites in rutile (Ti : O = 1 : 2), so the fifth oxygen must be accommodated.

Electronic compensation (low to moderate p_{\mathrm{O_2}}, high T):

\mathrm{Nb_2O_5} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{TiO_2}\ } 2\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}} + 4\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2e^{\prime}

Cation-vacancy compensation (high p_{\mathrm{O_2}}):

2\mathrm{Nb_2O_5} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{TiO_2}\ } 4\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Ti}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}} + 10\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}

Checks: sites 2 : 4 and 5 : 10; oxygen 5 = 4 + 1 and 10 = 10; charge +2 - 2 = 0 and +4 - 4 = 0.

With electronic compensation n = [\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}}], independent of p_{\mathrm{O_2}}, so Nb-doped \mathrm{TiO_2} is an n-type semiconductor; the electrons sit on \mathrm{Ti^{3+}} (\mathrm{Ti_{Ti}^{\prime}}). With vacancy compensation [\mathrm{Nb_{Ti}^{\bullet}}] = 4[\mathrm{V_{Ti}^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}}] and the oxide stays insulating.

Given: \mathrm{Fe_{1-y}O}, rock salt, a = 429\ \mathrm{pm} = 4.29\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}, \rho = 5.63\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.

Assumed: the oxygen sublattice is complete (4 O per cubic cell) and the deviation is taken up by Fe vacancies, as the slides show for wustite; M_{\mathrm{Fe}} = 55.85, M_{\mathrm{O}} = 16.00\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}, N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}.

Find: (i) y; (ii) the number of defects per unit volume.

Solution

\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{cell}} &= a^3 = (4.29\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm})^3 = 7.895\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ \rho V_{\mathrm{cell}} N_A &= 4\left[(1-y)M_{\mathrm{Fe}} + M_{\mathrm{O}}\right] \\ (5.63)(7.895\times10^{-23})(6.022\times10^{23}) &= 267.7\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}} \\ (1-y)(55.85) &= \frac{267.7}{4} - 16.00 = 50.92 \\ 1 - y &= 0.912, \qquad y = 0.088 \end{aligned}

Defects per cell and per volume:

\begin{aligned} [\mathrm{V_{Fe}^{\prime\prime}}] &= \frac{4y}{a^3} = \frac{4(0.0883)}{7.895\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}} = 4.47\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} \\ [\mathrm{Fe_{Fe}^{\bullet}}] &= 2[\mathrm{V_{Fe}^{\prime\prime}}] = 8.94\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} \end{aligned}

Each \mathrm{V_{Fe}^{\prime\prime}} is balanced by two \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} ions (holes), from \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \to \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_{Fe}^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}; so 2y/(1-y) = 19\% of the iron is \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}.

Answer: (i) \mathrm{Fe_{0.912}O} (y = 0.088); (ii) about 4.5\times10^{21} iron vacancies per \mathrm{cm^3}, with 8.9\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} per \mathrm{cm^3} (1.3\times10^{22} point defects in all).

8c.html:
Intrinsic defects are thermally activated. Making n defects costs enthalpy n\Delta H but gains configurational entropy, so G has a minimum at

\frac{n}{N} = \exp\left(\frac{\Delta S}{k}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H}{kT}\right)

Every crystal above 0 K therefore contains defects, and their number rises exponentially with T.

Pairs. For Schottky or Frenkel pairs the mass-action law and electroneutrality give [\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}] = [\mathrm{V_X^{\bullet\bullet}}] = \exp(-\Delta H/2kT). A plot of \ln[\mathrm{V}] against 1/T is a line of slope -\Delta H/2k. For NaCl (\Delta H_s = 2.3 eV) n_s/N rises from 4.8\times10^{-20} at 300 K to 3.6\times10^{-7} at 900 K; for MgO (7.5 eV) it is only 1.4\times10^{-15} even at 1273 K.

Dopants (extrinsic region). A dopant such as \mathrm{Cd_{Na}^{\bullet}} fixes its compensating defect: [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cd_{Na}^{\bullet}}] + [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{\bullet}}].

  • High T: intrinsic defects outnumber the dopant; slope -\Delta H_s/2k.
  • Low T: [\mathrm{V_{Na}^{\prime}}] = [\mathrm{Cd_{Na}^{\bullet}}], a plateau independent of T. The minority defect, [\mathrm{V_{Cl}^{\bullet}}] = K_s/[\mathrm{Cd_{Na}^{\bullet}}], falls with the steeper slope -\Delta H_s/k.
  • The knee lies where K_s^{1/2} equals the dopant level; more dopant moves it to higher T.

Non-stoichiometric and electronic defects. Every mass-action constant varies as K = K_0\exp(-\Delta H/kT). For example [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] = (K_v/4)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6} grows as \exp(-\Delta H_v/3kT), and n = p = \exp(-E_g/2kT) across the band gap.

Rapid quenching freezes in the high-temperature population; slow cooling lets defects anneal out or cluster.
